content: In pregnancies complicated by diabetes, the primary concerns during the third trimester are the risks of fetal distress and birth trauma, particularly due to fetal macrosomia, which refers to an excessively large fetus. This review aimed to evaluate the impact of a policy of elective delivery, as opposed to expectant management, on maternal and perinatal mortality and morbidity in diabetic pregnant women at term. The search for relevant studies was conducted through the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, with the initial search completed on July 24, 2004, and an update performed on July 24, 2009. The updated results were added to a section awaiting classification. The review included all randomized controlled trials that compared elective delivery, either through labor induction or elective cesarean section, with expectant management in term diabetic pregnancies. The data from the only available trial were independently analyzed by three reviewers to assess maternal and perinatal outcomes. The results were presented as relative risks (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The trial included 200 women with insulin-requiring diabetes, most of whom had gestational diabetes, while 13 participants had pre-existing type 2 diabetes (classified as class B). The study compared active induction of labor at 38 weeks of gestation with expectant management up to 42 weeks. The findings showed no statistically significant difference in the risk of cesarean section between the two groups (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.52–1.26). However, the risk of macrosomia was significantly reduced in the group that underwent active induction of labor (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.32–0.98). In the expectant management group, three cases of mild shoulder dystocia were reported, but no other perinatal morbidities were observed. The authors concluded that the results of this single randomized controlled trial suggest that induction of labor at 38 weeks in insulin-requiring diabetic women reduces the risk of macrosomia. However, there was no significant difference in maternal or neonatal morbidity between the two groups. Due to the rarity of maternal and neonatal complications and the limited number of participants in the trial, definitive conclusions cannot be drawn. Future studies should explore women's perspectives on elective delivery versus prolonged surveillance and insulin treatment. Additionally, the single citation awaiting classification in this review may influence the conclusions once it is assessed.
